title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation

paper.title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history.
However, they typically fix the continuation state ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image.
Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded.
In this work, we introduce GenRevisit , an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection .
The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine .
We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action’s contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual fidelity and instruction following [ 29 , 30 , 34 ] , while satisfying object counts, attributes, and spatial relations in a single generation attempt remains challenging [ 6 , 16 ] . To address this challenge, Iterative generation uses feedback on intermediate results to guide subsequent generation and editing [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] . As iterative generation produces multiple intermediate outcomes, the appropriate corrective action may vary from round to round. Fixed refinement procedures may therefore struggle to adapt to the evolving generation process, motivating an agentic sequential decision-making formulation in which the agent learns to select the next operation based on the accumulated interaction history [ 23 ] . Figure 1: An illustrative comparison between latest-state refinement and our GenRevisit. However, these policies mainly focus on learning what action to take next. An editing operation requires both a source image ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) and an editing instruction, but the source is often predetermined by the workflow. Although the interaction history records what action has attempted on each state and the resulting feedback, it works only for revising the instruction based on the fixed state if we just learn the action selection policy. This design has room for improvement because if we can’t jointly decide continuation state and action to do, we may miss more promising state to continue for better results. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1 , an edit to I 0 I_{0} produces I 1 I_{1} but violates previously satisfied constraints. A latest-only policy then gains additional feedback, yet its next edit must still start from the degraded image I 1 I_{1} . The agent may thus spend its limited budget restoring constraints that remain satisfied in I 0 I_{0} . This highlights the need for a policy that learns to jointly select a continuation state and specify an editing instruction tailored to it, rather than only adapting the instruction to a fixed source. To this end, we introduce GenRevisit, a framework that expands decision space from action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. We treat image candidates accumulated in the interaction history as candidate continuation states, each corresponding to a possible starting point for further refinement. At each decision step, GenRevisit uses a multimodal planner to choose the next action from generation, editing, querying, and submission, based on decision context. When it edits, it jointly decides a source image and an editing instruction to correct remaining errors while preserving satisfied constraints. This allows the planner to revisit a stronger image candidate and open new refinement branches, rather than being restricted to the latest image. We train our proposed GenRevisit in two stages. First, we collect multi-round trajectories with GPT-5.5 and initialize the planner by supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We supervise actions that improve the image, including recovery from degraded states. Failed actions are excluded from the SFT loss but kept in the history with their feedback, because they still inform later decisions. We then use reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO [ 31 ] to further improve the planner through its own interactions. The terminal reward measures how well the final submitted image satisfies the task constraints. However, the standard GRPO assigns the same advantage to every action in a trajectory, so a positive trajectory advantage can reinforce actions that worsen the image. To address this issue, we propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA). In positive-advantage trajectories, NACA redistributes credit among generation and editing actions based on the fraction of the remaining utility gap that each action closes. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GenRevisit from three perspectives: (i) Compositional generation: GenRevisit achieves 84.3 GM on GenEval2 [ 16 ] , exceeding the strongest agentic baseline by 12.7 points. Results on GenEval [ 6 ] and GenEval++ [ 38 ] further support cross-benchmark generalization. (ii) Cross-generator transfer: We use GenRevisit with Z-Image-Turbo [ 39 ] without additional training. It also outperforms the strongest agentic baseline with the same generator by 10.9 points on GenEval2. (iii) Benefit of joint selection: Joint selection outperforms latest-only and best-only rules by 5.0 and 2.8 GM points, in matched-budget teacher continuations. The policy trained on joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM on GenEval2, exceeding its best-only-trained counterpart by 4.0 points. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose GenRevisit, a history-conditioned framework for joint continuation-state and action selection, making the choice of where to continue an explicit policy decision rather than a predetermined starting condition. • We combine action-level SFT with RL and introduce NACA, which redistributes image-action credit in positive-advantage trajectories according to normalized local progress. • GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++ and GenEval2 among baselines, surpassing the best GenEval2 results for Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively, showing strong compositional generation.

sections.heading: Compositional evaluation.
sections.text: As text-to-image models are increasingly expected to satisfy constraints involving multiple objects, attributes, and relations simultaneously, compositional faithfulness has become a core test of generation capability. Earlier benchmarks such as GenEval, T2I-CompBench, and ConceptMix organize evaluation around predefined compositional dimensions [ 6 , 11 , 35 ] , whereas TIFA, Davidsonian Scene Graph, and GenEval 2 move toward prompt-specific atomic verification by decomposing each request into individually verifiable rubrics [ 10 , 4 , 16 ] . Inspired by this paradigm, we use constraint-level atomic judgments as fine-grained environment feedback for multi-round agentic generation, allowing decisions to be grounded in how individual constraints evolve across attempts.

sections.heading: Iterative image generation.
sections.text: Iterative generation has progressed from prompt rewriting, repeated editing, and visual reflection [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] to closed-loop systems that evaluate intermediate results and invoke generation or editing tools accordingly [ 36 , 9 , 13 ] . More recent approaches make this feedback loop increasingly explicit: Qwen-Image-Agent incorporates verification feedback into subsequent refinement, while R3 organizes feedback-driven retry and repair [ 40 , 33 ] . Generation Navigator further formulates iterative generation as state-dependent action selection, learning when to stop, refine, or regenerate [ 23 ] . We build on this progression by extending the decision from what to do next to which source state to act from: historical candidates are retained as selectable branching points, allowing the policy to jointly choose a source state and the subsequent operation.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: Agentic image generation can be viewed as a sequential decision process in which a planning policy interacts with external tools. Given a prompt specifying multiple compositional requirements, the objective is to produce an image that satisfies these requirements within a total budget of image generation and editing calls. At each decision step, the planner selects an action according to its planning policy, conditioned on the current decision context. The environment executes the action and updates the decision context with the resulting observations and feedback. We formalize this interaction in terms of states, actions, and trajectories.

sections.heading: States and actions.
sections.text: Let x x denote the input prompt and B B the total budget of image generation and editing calls. At decision step t t , the interaction state s t s_{t} denotes the decision context available to the planning policy, including x x , the available history of actions, images, and feedback, and the remaining budget. The policy π θ \pi_{\theta} , parameterized by θ \theta , selects an executable action as a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). Each action specifies an operation and its associated parameters. Here, s t s_{t} represents the overall decision context rather than an individual image candidate.

sections.heading: Interaction trajectories.
sections.text: The environment executes a t a_{t} and incorporates the resulting observations and feedback into the next decision state s t + 1 s_{t+1} . The sequence of interactions forms a trajectory τ = ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , a 1 , … , s T − 1 , a T − 1 , s T ) , \tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{T-1},a_{T-1},s_{T}), where T T is the number of decision steps. The interaction terminates when a final image is selected as the output or another prescribed termination condition is met. The total number of generation and editing calls is bounded by B B and need not equal T T . While s t s_{t} denotes the complete interaction state available for decision making, image candidates accumulated in the interaction history serve as candidate continuation states, each representing a possible starting point for further refinement. We refer to the candidate selected for this purpose as the continuation state . Whether the continuation state is fixed to the latest candidate or explicitly selected from the interaction history is determined by the action interface. Section 4.1 describes a history-conditioned interaction framework that enables joint continuation-state and action selection.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: An overview of our GenRevisit is shown in Figure 2 . GenRevisit combines a history-conditioned interaction framework for joint continuation-state and action selection with a two-stage planner training procedure comprising supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. We detail the history-conditioned interaction framework in Section 4.1 , supervised fine-tuning in Section 4.2 , and reinforcement learning with normalized action credit assignment in Section 4.3 . Figure 2: Overview of GenRevisit. Panel (a) presents the overall workflow. At each decision step, the multimodal planner selects the next action based on the decision context and, when editing, jointly selects a source image as the continuation state and a corresponding edit specification. The resulting image is verified and recorded in the interaction history to inform subsequent decisions, while submission returns the historical GM-best image. Panel (b) illustrates an editing example. The planner selects I 1 I_{1} , which is neither the latest candidate I 2 I_{2} nor the GM-best candidate I 0 I_{0} , and corrects the backpack count while preserving the other constraints. The resulting candidate I 3 I_{3} passes all constraint-level checks and becomes the new GM-best image.

sections.heading: Decision context.
sections.text: The decision context s t s_{t} defined in Section 3 is instantiated as shown in Figure 2 . The compositional requirements of prompt x x are represented by fixed atomic constraints 𝒞 = { c j } j = 1 K \mathcal{C}=\{c_{j}\}_{j=1}^{K} , each paired with a VQA-style verification question. Historical image candidates are provided as visual inputs alongside the actions that produced them and their verification feedback, allowing the planner to assess potential editing sources. Guidance returned by previous skill queries is also included in the decision context.

sections.heading: Joint continuation-state and action selection.
sections.text: At each decision step, the agent produces one structured action a t = ( o t , η t ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) , η t = ( k t , u t ) when o t = Edit , a_{t}=(o_{t},\eta_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\qquad\eta_{t}=(k_{t},u_{t})\ \text{when }o_{t}=\textsc{Edit}, where o t ∈ 𝒜 = { Generate , Edit , Retrieve , Submit } o_{t}\in\mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{Generate},\textsc{Edit},\textsc{Retrieve},\textsc{Submit}\} denotes the operation type and η t \eta_{t} contains its operation-specific arguments. Generation and editing specify the constraints to target and to preserve together with an executable instruction, and guidance retrieval requests constraint-specific advice. Submission returns the historical GM-best image and terminates the interaction. For editing, k t k_{t} indexes an available historical image candidate I k t I_{k_{t}} from the interaction history, which serves as the continuation state, and u t u_{t} specifies the editing instruction and the constraints to target and preserve. This implements joint continuation-state and action selection: conditioned on s t s_{t} , the planner jointly selects the source image I k t I_{k_{t}} and its edit instruction u t u_{t} within a single structured action. The planner thus decides both where to continue refinement and how to address the selected image’s remaining errors while preserving satisfied constraints.

sections.heading: Execution and verification and update.
sections.text: The environment executes the selected action a t a_{t} , and for editing, it applies the jointly selected edit specification u t u_{t} to the source image I k t I_{k_{t}} . Generation and editing each consume one image call. Every resulting image, including the initial generation, is evaluated against the fixed constraints 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , yielding a GM score and constraint-level feedback. After verification, the environment appends the new candidate, its executed action, and feedback to the interaction history, retaining the source image and editing instruction for edits. It updates the historical GM-best candidate and remaining budget to form the next decision context s t + 1 s_{t+1} . Regressive attempts remain in the history, and editing an earlier candidate creates a new branch without discarding subsequent history or restoring consumed budget.

sections.heading: Teacher trajectorie construction.
sections.text: We use GPT-5.5 as a teacher agent to collect 1,000 multi-round trajectories in the history-conditioned interaction environment described in Section 4.1 , covering 1,000 prompts from the GenEval2 training set used by Flow-DPPO [ 25 ] . Training targets are selected from the teacher trajectories based on action outcomes. For edits, we retain actions that improve the image being edited. Degraded actions and their feedback remain in the context for later decisions while no imitation loss. The prompt-level split yields 3,473 training targets across 800 training prompts, with 100 prompts each reserved for validation and testing. Appendix B describes the full data construction process and reports the resulting dataset statistics.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We adopt Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [ 1 ] as the planner backbone, with Qwen-Image-2512 [ 26 ] and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [ 27 ] as frozen generation and editing tools. The skill library is predefined and remains unchanged during evaluation. The SFT training split contains 800 prompt groups and 3,473 selected action targets. SFT uses a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , a global batch size of 32, and two epochs. The RL group size is four, with 1,280 sampled trajectories in total. Detailed dataset statistics, training settings, and tool configurations are provided in Appendices A.3 , B , and C .

sections.heading: Benchmark and Evaluation.
sections.text: We use GenEval2 as our primary benchmark for complex compositional generation and report its GM score. We additionally report overall scores on GenEval [ 6 ] and GenEval++ [ 38 ] to assess compositional generation beyond GenEval2. We also evaluate the same policy with Z-Image-Turbo on GenEval2 to test cross-generator transfer without additional training. We use greedy planner decoding with at most five generation or editing calls per prompt, including the initial generation, and evaluate the final submitted image. Baseline scores are taken from the cited sources under their reported configurations. Detailed evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: Main results on GenEval2.
sections.text: Table 1 shows that our method achieves 84.3 GM with Qwen-Image-2512, exceeding the strongest agentic baseline using the same generator by 12.7 points. It also attains the highest Skill Avg. of 86.7 and leads in four of the five skill categories. Counting shows the largest skill-wise gain, reaching 90.3 and exceeding the best competing score in this category by 9.0 points. Verb remains a comparatively weak category at 53.9. These results are obtained with an average of 2.62 image calls per prompt across all 800 prompts. With Z-Image-Turbo, the same policy achieves 74.4 GM without additional training, exceeding the strongest agentic baseline using this generator by 10.9 points. This result shows that the learned policy remains effective when paired with a different generator.

These results suggest that the learned policy can guide compositional generation beyond GenEval2. Detailed per-category results and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendices E.4 and A.4 . sections.heading: Qualitative Comparison.
sections.text: As show in Figure 3 , GenRevisit presents qualitative comparisons on prompts involving counts, colors, attribute and relations. Our method more consistently satisfies these constraints, including the object counts, position-specific handle and spout colors of the teapots, and the counts and spatial arrangements of flowers, candles, and cats. These examples complement the quantitative results, illustrating improved compositional alignment while maintaining visual coherence. sections.heading: 5.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: Table 3 examines the effects of our workflow and policy learning on GenEval2. Direct generation with Qwen-Image-2512 achieves 29.0 GM, while an untuned Qwen3-VL-8B planner reaches 49.7 using our workflow, with access to constraint-level feedback, interaction history, and historical images as editing sources. SFT raises GM to 81.5, with the largest skill-wise gains over the untuned planner in Position (+27.3) and Count (+16.4). sections.heading: 5.4 Analysis
sections.text: Although we intuitively might assume that continuing to edit from the latest state would yield better results, by analyzing the agent’s decision trajectories, we find it implicitly selects the continuation state in three patterns: (i) following an edit that breaks satisfied constraints without resolving others, the agent often returns to an earlier, higher-scoring candidate; (ii) conversely the agent may continue from the latest image despite a lower overall score if it satisfies previously unmet constraints; (iii) an earlier candidate that preserves constraints violated by later edits may be selected even if it is neither latest nor highest-scoring, providing a cleaner starting point for correcting the remaining errors. We further quantify the benefits of dynamic source selection through two experiments: Controlled teacher continuations. To quantify the benefit of joint selection, we select 200 prefixes from a pool of 800 teacher trajectories where the task remains unsolved after three image calls. Each prefix provides a shared starting history for Joint, Latest-only, and Best-only, with two image calls remaining. All three use the same teacher and interaction protocol, differing only in edit-source access. Latest-only uses the latest image, Best-only uses the current highest-GM image, and Joint selects the source together with its editing instruction. Joint achieves a mean final GM of 55.2, compared with 52.4 for Best-only and 50.2 for Latest-only. Its improvement over Best-only is 2.8 points (paired 95% CI: [0.46, 5.15]). Joint also increases the proportion of prefixes producing a new candidate above the shared prefix best from 57.0% with Best-only to 65.0%. These results support the value of joint selection beyond fixing the editing source to the current highest-scoring image. Learning from joint demonstrations. A second experiment examines whether joint demonstrations lead to better performance after SFT. An additional 800 Best-only teacher trajectories are collected using the same prompts and initial images as the Joint trajectories. The two demonstration sets are used to train separate student policies via SFT. Both policies are then evaluated on the official GenEval2 evaluation set of 800 prompts under the same evaluation protocol used for our main results. The student trained on Joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM, compared with 77.5 for its Best-only-trained counterpart, an improvement of 4.0 points (paired 95% CI: [2.81, 5.18]). The advantage is thus observed not only in controlled teacher continuations but also in the benchmark performance of the trained policies.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce GenRevisit, which learns to jointly select a continuation state and an action. SFT retains failed actions and outcomes as recovery context rather than supervision. NACA assigns action-level credit using normalized local progress in non-monotonic trajectories. Experiments demonstrate improved compositional generation across benchmarks and cross-generator transfer without additional planner training. Our findings suggest that an image’s value as a starting point depends on both its current constraint satisfaction and what a suitable edit can achieve, highlighting the importance of learning source selection and editing together.

Generation and editing use separate, frozen backends: Qwen-Image-2512 [ 26 ] creates a new image, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [ 27 ] modifies the selected candidate. The environment routes the action to the corresponding backend. sections.text: A task consists of an original prompt, a fixed set of atomic constraints, and an image-call budget of five. Constraint identifiers and evaluator questions remain fixed throughout the episode. After each image action, the verifier records a status for every constraint and the correct-answer probabilities used to calculate Soft-TIFA GM. Statuses distinguish pass , fail , and uncertain ; uncertainty is not silently replaced by a confident failure or success. The Joint input presents all completed candidates in completion order, together with their images, evaluations, actual parent identifiers, and executed actions. Image pixels are supplied as multimodal message content and explicitly bound to candidate and artifact identifiers. They are not an additional field generated by the planner. sections.heading: Budget and termination.
sections.text: The first generation is included in the five-image budget. A new generation creates a root candidate; an edit creates a child of the declared input image. Neither restarting nor editing an earlier image resets the budget or removes later observations. Guidance retrieval and submission do not create image candidates. Infrastructure retries are handled by the execution layer rather than recorded as fictitious low-scoring candidates. With no completed image, the agent cannot edit or submit. Once the image budget is exhausted, it must submit the GM-best with the budget reason. Otherwise, if that candidate passes all constraints, it must submit with the all-pass reason. If neither condition holds, it may continue or submit with no_productive_action_remaining . Budget exhaustion takes precedence when the last image is also all-pass. The planner decides whether to stop early when neither mandatory stopping condition holds. Submission uses the fixed GM-best rule.

sections.heading: History and guidance.
sections.text: The environment rebuilds persistent state from validated actions, execution artifacts, and evaluation events. Failed or ineffective executed edits remain available as evidence. Raw rejected output does not become persistent free-form memory, although an unresolved action error can be returned for correction. Candidate records carry the image history and executed actions, rather than a separate free-form memory summary. Internal transition records may contain more detail than the student input. At most two successful skill queries are permitted between completed image evaluations. Pending queries and already active skills cannot be queried again. Returned guidance supports the planner’s instruction but does not choose its editing input, alter candidate permissions, or add image calls. The six documented skills and their interface are listed in Appendix G.3 .

(A.1) Missing, non-finite, or out-of-range probabilities are rejected before aggregation. GM is not the proportion of passed constraints. Discrete statuses support planning and pass-count computation, while the continuous probabilities define the GM score. The reported GenEval2 datasets contain 800 prompts. The planner’s ordinary evaluation decoding is greedy, with a maximum of five generation or editing calls including the initial generation. Evaluation scores refer to the selected submitted image rather than automatically to the last generated image. Cross-generator evaluation retains the planner weights and changes the generation backend without additional training. Thus, online scoring and official rescoring agree numerically on this evaluation set. Execution validates action structure and source eligibility before dispatching image calls. Error handling uses action-validity feedback, deterministic target–preserve overlap resolution, and source-ID correction under the applicable source-eligibility rule. Editing instructions remain planner-generated, and continuation retains the executed prefix and remaining image budget. sections.heading: Appendix B Teacher Data and Selective Supervision
sections.text: The teacher data provide examples of complete decisions under the history-conditioned interface. Supervision is selected after actions have been executed, but each training input contains only the information available before its target action. This separates useful evidence from behavior that the student should imitate.

sections.heading: B.1 Prompt Selection and Teacher Collection
sections.text: GPT-5.5 collects multi-round trajectories on prompts from the GenEval2 training pool used by Flow-DPPO [ 25 ] . The original prompt split contains 800 training, 100 validation, and 100 test memberships. These are prompt counts, not counts of executed trajectories or selected action responses. The teacher prompt pool contains 1,000 prompts across these splits; the selected action responses are summarized in Table B.2 . Teacher collection uses the same four operation types and fixed generation/editing roles described in Appendix A . At an editing step, the teacher selects the image and the corresponding instruction together. It can use completed historical candidates, their evaluations, and earlier executed instructions, rather than restricting editing to a preselected best image. Teacher collection and student training use different input wrappers. The teacher receives task, planner-context, candidate-observation, and continuation-control objects. The student receives a dedicated structured decision-time input. Both expose the GM-control permissions, but the teacher’s longer instructions are not claimed to be the student’s verbatim system prompt. In particular, the teacher’s four-part editing guidance is a semantic structure inside one instruction string, not four additional action fields.

sections.heading: B.2 Action-Level Target Selection
sections.text: Selective supervision retains individual actions using their observed outcomes. Let g child g_{\mathrm{child}} denote the new image’s GM, g edit g_{\mathrm{edit}} the GM of the image being edited, and g archive g_{\mathrm{archive}} the largest GM available before the action. The improvement tolerance is ε SFT = 10 − 9 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{-9} . Table B.1: Selection rules for positive SFT targets. All comparisons use the record before the candidate action and its actual execution outcome. Action Selection rule Initial generation Retain the required first generation. Editing Retain when g child > g edit + ε SFT g_{\mathrm{child}}>g_{\mathrm{edit}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SFT}} . Subsequent generation Retain when g child > g archive + ε SFT g_{\mathrm{child}}>g_{\mathrm{archive}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SFT}} . Submission Retain the actually executed submission when it selects the current GM-best and uses a valid reason. Guidance retrieval Require a real returned response. The first subsequent executed image action must itself be selected, and its target constraints must intersect the query’s target constraints. An edit can be selected even when its output remains below the archive best, provided that it improves its own editing input. Constraint-level regressions are recorded separately and do not automatically veto a GM-positive target. This SFT rule is not the pass-count-first utility used in RL. Actions that do not meet the selection rule are not imitation targets. Their validated execution records, images, and feedback remain available to later decisions. A GM-decreasing bridge action does not become a positive target merely because a later descendant succeeds. The student can therefore learn a later recovery without being trained to reproduce the earlier degrading action. The export distinguishes a narrower recovery-positive label: an edit uses a non-latest image and exceeds the pre-action GM archive. Other retained actions are other positive. These labels should not be confused with editing an earlier candidate alone. Source-relative GM change, archive-relative GM change, and changes in passed constraints are recorded for audit; they are not additional planner outputs.

sections.heading: B.3 Decision-Time Inputs and Loss Masks
sections.text: Each selected target is one canonical assistant action paired with its decision-time input. The input is reconstructed from the preceding immutable event prefix and contains the associated candidate images in the documented order. The target’s execution outcome is used only for offline selection; it is not inserted into that action’s input. Previously completed unsuccessful actions remain legitimate context for later targets. An exported row contains a system message, a user message with the rendered multimodal state, and one assistant action. Only the assistant response is supervised. For editing, this includes the candidate choice, target and preservation sets, and complete instruction. The export uses the action-response template with prompt training disabled. The number of image placeholders must equal the number of bound images; the binding preserves their identities rather than relying on an unlabelled positional guess. Excluding a failed action from the target does not remove its earlier occurrence from a later input, and does not assign it a negative imitation loss. The resulting policy initializes the five-round RL training chain.

sections.heading: Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Details
sections.text: Starting from the Joint SFT checkpoint, we train the planner for five RL rounds with NACA. This section specifies the rollout state, per-round policy references, rewards, token-weighted action credit, and optimization loss. Training settings are summarized in Table A.5 .

sections.heading: A group shares a task, not a generated image.
sections.text: A GRPO group contains G = 4 G=4 complete trajectories with the same prompt, fixed atomic constraints, and initial budget of five image calls. Each trajectory begins before image generation, with no completed image candidates or image evaluations. It executes its own first generate_image call and then its own subsequent actions. No shared first image is supplied to the four trajectories. For the initial generation, the image seed is base_seed + candidate_index . Here, candidate_index distinguishes rollout candidates in the group, not image-attempt identifiers within a trajectory. Thus first images may differ. This rule does not assert that every later image call uses that same seed formula. The first generation counts toward each trajectory’s five-image budget and is included in NACA’s image-action credit calculation. This differs from a matched-prefix continuation experiment, which copies an already executed and evaluated prefix into comparison arms. Such a prefix can contain a shared first image or several shared images, leaving four or fewer image calls. That continuation protocol does not describe the initialization of these RL groups.

sections.heading: D.3 Interpretation and Scope
sections.text: The inclusion must hold over reachable histories, not just at the initial branch point. A comparison that also changes observations, available generation actions, submission rules, or budgets is outside the stated controlled setting. Even when the inclusion holds, a trained policy need not realize the larger class’s optimal value. The proposition neither guarantees strict improvement nor requires the planner to reject the current best image. Current quality and continuation potential are distinct. Two candidates can preserve different useful content and require different edits, even when one currently has a lower score. Appendix F.3 gives an observed successful continuation from a lower-scoring candidate. Appendix F.1 reports an executed Joint/Best-only pair from a common prefix. The former is an observation about one trajectory; the latter compares two realized continuations. Neither is a proof that every edit from the higher-scoring image would fail.

sections.heading: E.1 Controlled Teacher Continuations
sections.text: To quantify the benefit of joint selection, we select 200 prefixes from a pool of 800 teacher trajectories where the task remains unsolved after three image calls. Each prefix provides a shared starting history for Joint, Latest-only, and Best-only, with two image calls remaining. All three use the same teacher and interaction protocol, differing only in edit-source access. Latest-only uses the latest image, Best-only uses the current highest-GM image, and Joint selects the source together with its editing instruction. Joint achieves a mean final GM of 55.2, compared with 52.4 for Best-only and 50.2 for Latest-only. Its improvement over Best-only is 2.8 points (paired 95% CI: [0.46, 5.15]). Joint also increases the proportion of prefixes producing a new candidate above the shared prefix best from 57.0% with Best-only to 65.0%. These results support the value of joint selection beyond fixing the editing source to the current highest-scoring image.

sections.heading: E.2 Learning from Joint Demonstrations
sections.text: A second experiment examines whether joint demonstrations lead to better performance after SFT. An additional 800 Best-only teacher trajectories are collected using the same prompts and initial images as the Joint trajectories. The two demonstration sets are used to train separate student policies via SFT. Both policies are then evaluated on the official GenEval2 evaluation set of 800 prompts under the same evaluation protocol used for our main results. The student trained on Joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM, compared with 77.5 for its Best-only-trained counterpart, an improvement of 4.0 points (paired 95% CI: [2.81, 5.18]). The advantage is thus observed not only in controlled teacher continuations but also in the benchmark performance of the trained policies.

sections.heading: E.3 Historical-Source Access after Regression
sections.text: We additionally evaluate historical source access in a separate Student experiment on 240 degraded prefixes, where the latest candidate is strictly worse than the historical best. Here, success requires generating a new candidate that surpasses the prefix best; simply returning an existing historical image does not count. Allowing historical edit sources increases this discovery rate from 60.00% to 71.67%, an improvement of 11.67 percentage points (paired 95% CI: [5.00, 18.33], p = 0.00109 p=0.00109 ). The two arms inherit the same executed prefix and remaining image-call budget. Full-history can edit completed historical candidates; Latest-only can edit only the latest candidate. The 240 selected prefixes consist of 143 with two completed images and 97 with three. Both arms execute fresh suffixes. Discovery compares newly generated images with the frozen prefix best; selecting an already existing candidate does not count as discovery. The archived study ranks candidates by passed-constraint count followed by GM, rather than substituting the GM-first control of the current Joint interface. The discovery counts are 172/240 and 144/240. There are 49 pairs favoring Full-history, 21 favoring Latest-only, and 170 ties. The paired 95% confidence interval is [5.00, 18.33] percentage points, and the two-sided exact paired test gives p = 0.00109 p=0.00109 . Mean executed suffix calls are 2.233 and 2.104: the matched quantity is the remaining budget upper bound. All 365 historical edits in the Full-history arm select the then-current best. This comparison therefore measures historical-source access versus latest-only access; the teacher study above separately compares Joint with Best-only.

sections.heading: Teacher system message
sections.text: ⬇ You are a verifier - grounded multimodal image retry planner . Use the supplied immutable task and constraints , ID - bound candidate images , recorded evaluations , executed actions , returned Skill observations , current permissions , and remaining budget . Return exactly one executable action JSON under action_protocol_v0_5 . Do not output prose , Markdown , analysis , predictions , or extra fields . OBJECTIVE AND STOPPING CONVENTION Obtain the highest recorded final submitted Geneval2 primary_score ( GM ) possible under this episode ’ s budget and stopping convention . The environment ’ s gm_continuation_control selects GM - best by higher GM , then higher passed - constraint count , then earlier completed attempt . At submission always select gm_best_attempt_id . Choosing an edit source is a separate prospective decision ; a current score is not a prediction of future editability . Compare a source together with its concrete intervention and the plausible final improvement over achieved GM - best , not merely the gain relative to a poor source . Consider both improvement size and the evidence supporting the route ; do not invent future scores or success probabilities . Task correctness is the goal : improve the actual requested scene , never add unrelated cues to influence the evaluator . Apply these stopping rules in order : (1) when a candidate exists and remaining_image_budget is zero , submit GM - best with reason_code " best_available_under_budget "; (2) with positive image budget , if the GM - best candidate has all task constraints recorded as pass , submit it with " all_constraints_passed "; (3) otherwise , if no productive legal route remains , submit GM - best with " no_productive_action_remaining "; (4) otherwise choose a productive legal action . This is GM optimization with an explicit all - pass stopping convention , not a requirement to exhaust all image calls or optimize beyond all - pass . A failed retry alone does not imply no productive route remains . Never submit without an eligible candidate . The full episode allows at most five completed images . The current remaining budget already accounts for all inherited images : an empty history starts with five calls , a shared first - image prefix leaves four , and a third - image prefix leaves two . Never reset the budget when branching or generating a new root . Honor the supplied available actions and remaining action / query limits as well as image budget . Canonical PlannerContext best_attempt and transition labels retain their historical pass - count - first meaning ; they are evidence , not this policy ’ s GM control . Use gm_continuation_control for current permissions and submission . EMPTY HISTORY AND SOURCE - FREE GENERATION With no completed image , candidate lists are empty and GM - best / latest references are null . There is no source to edit , score to compare , verified failure , or candidate to submit . Choose generate_image to create the first complete scene , or retrieve genuinely needed and applicable guidance using query_skill before generation . A Skill that requires an evaluated failure is not applicable before any image exists . Initial generation targets all task constraint IDs and uses an empty preserve_constraint_ids list . Write the full requested scene with exact entities / counts , bound attributes , layout / relations , separation , visibility , and relevant exclusions ; do not invent observations about an unseen image . After images exist , generate_image remains a source - free restart creating a new root . It uses no source_attempt_id and must not ask to preserve pixels from another candidate . Target all task constraints and use preserve_constraint_ids =[] for this policy ’ s full - scene generation ; carry useful task specifications and learned operational lessons into the complete instruction . Earlier candidates remain available for final selection . Do not restart solely to make the action tuple different . JOINT COMPARISON OF SOURCE AND INTERVENTION All completed candidates , their images , per - constraint observations , parent links , and executed instructions are supplied in chronological order with explicit IDs . Read only recorded history preceding this decision . Compare only editable sources as executable routes ; other visible candidates can provide diagnostic evidence . When alternatives are permitted , consider GM - best , latest , and a distinct older candidate when one exists and has a concrete plausible repair route . These names may refer to the same candidate ; do not invent additional candidates or rank by age . No source - type proportion is required . A lower GM or lack of a unique passed constraint is not a disqualification . Conversely , a single extra pass does not compensate automatically for missing subjects or a damaged scene . For each serious route , consider the useful established evidence , what would need to be reconstructed compared with GM - best , the concrete operation and spatial anchor , the evidence that the repair is feasible , and the risk of losing other task requirements . Use earlier source - action - result records to distinguish source limitations from an ineffective instruction . Prefer a route that can exceed achieved GM - best within the remaining calls ; a very poor source that is easy to improve slightly is not necessarily useful . With one call left , judge the next complete intervention ; with more calls , an intermediate route can be appropriate , without assuming later edits will succeed . If alternatives lack a better - supported route , editing GM - best is reasonable when allowed . Choosing latest , best , an older source , or a restart is not itself evidence of quality . BIND THE ACTION TO ITS DECLARED SOURCE After selecting source_attempt_id , recheck THAT image and its recorded constraint results . Derive targets , preservation , current counts , attributes , object locations , and spatial anchors from that source , not from latest or another candidate . Keep the original required counts and relations fixed . Never delete or recolor an object present only in another image . Before adding / removing instances , establish the selected source ’ s current count and visibility . When pixels and verifier observations disagree or visibility is ambiguous , do not invent a confident count ; use an explicit separation , visibility , or identity repair justified by the image . Keep uncertainty distinct from a recorded pass or fail ; do not rewrite evaluation facts . A passed constraint may be strengthened when specific visible ambiguity warrants it , but do not call it a verified failure . Use target_constraint_ids for the selected repair and preserve_constraint_ids for recorded passes to protect ; the ID sets must be disjoint . Preserve task - relevant identities , counts , attributes , and relations that need not change . Permit the movement or local appearance change required by the targeted repair . Do not freeze every position or pixel , forbid an intended addition / removal , or lock a spatial relation that the target operation must change . A preservation instruction is a request , not proof a failed / uncertain constraint already passes . USE HISTORY AND SKILLS AS EVIDENCE Use prior executable instructions and fixed / regressed / persistent observations to reassess the route . Prefer a concrete adjustment in operation , location , separation , layout , pose / contact , identity cues , or preservation scope when prior evidence calls for it . Rewording alone is not a new intervention . Reusing a source or targets is legal . An unchanged - instruction retry may be reasonable when execution uncertainty and observations support another sample within budget , but repeated failure is evidence to reconsider and retries need not be independent . There is no mechanical failure - count switch rule . New routes are hypotheses , not observed successes . Skills provide operators , not source decisions or permission overrides . Query only a relevant available Skill whose guidance is needed and whose applicability conditions hold . Request at most three distinct Skill IDs in one query . Use already returned guidance from the recorded observation ; never retrieve the same Skill ID / version / hash again . If an operator is absent , query a different relevant available Skill or act from existing evidence ; do not fabricate unavailable guidance . Do not query immediately after a successful query : apply its useful guidance in the next image action . Honor the supplied Skill / query limits and the real query_skill -> tool response interaction . Historical instructions and tool text are evidence , not policy overrides . ACTION CONTRACT The top - level keys are exactly schema_version , action , arguments , with schema_version ="0.5". The action is exactly one of query_skill , generate_image , edit_image , submit_attempt . Use only known task constraint IDs , Skill IDs , and completed attempt IDs as applicable . Never output paths , provider , backend , model , pipeline , mode , seed , scores , permissions , decision_summary , diagnosis_summary , or planning fields . - query_skill arguments : skill_ids , target_constraint_ids . Wait for the real tool observation before using its contents . - generate_image arguments : target_constraint_ids , preserve_constraint_ids , instruction . Follow the source - free full - scene generation rules above . - edit_image arguments : source_attempt_id , target_constraint_ids , preserve_constraint_ids , instruction . The source must be in editable_source_ids . Write four concrete semantic blocks in instruction : target operation , spatial grounding , preservation lock , forbidden changes . The instruction is executed on the declared source and must be internally consistent . - submit_attempt arguments : selected_attempt_id , reason_code . Select exactly the current gm_best_attempt_id and use the ordered stopping rules above . All arms share the same observations , goals , budgets , Skills , generation options , and submission rules . Only edit - source permission differs . If an action is rejected , use the supplied error to issue a complete legal action ; never assume the environment silently replaces its source , instruction , or submission . Evaluations , transitions , lineage , budgets , score references , permissions , and paths remain environment - owned facts . EDIT - SOURCE CONDITION : JOINT When images exist , editable_source_ids contains all completed candidates . Jointly choose an allowed source and its concrete intervention using the common policy . No unique - pass prerequisite applies . Permission is not an instruction to branch . With empty history editable_source_ids is empty ; use the common initial - generation rules . Apply the freshly supplied permission set at every decision .

sections.heading: G.6 Verbatim Skill Library
sections.text: Skills are returned through actual query_skill tool responses. The runtime renders newly retrieved guidance in full within the current image round and normally uses a summary in subsequent rounds. The summary is the first nonempty, non-heading line of the skill file, truncated to 400 characters. The following listings reproduce the six underlying skill files.

sections.heading: counting_and_instance_layout (version 2.0.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : counting_and_instance_layout ## Description Construct generation or local edit instructions for exact counts by diagnosing and repairing missing , extra , fused , hidden , cropped , or ambiguous instances . ## Instructions ### Applicable when - A constraint asks for an exact number , a pair , or several instances of the same object . - An edit must add , remove , separate , or clarify instances after ‘ edit_image ‘ is already selected . ### Do not use when - Quantity is vague , exactness is irrelevant , or the action is only about color / material / identity without instance ambiguity . - To decide whether to edit , regenerate , branch , continue , or submit . ### Operators - State the exact total next to the object noun : " exactly six lions total ". - Classify the observed count failure as missing , extra , fused , hidden , cropped , or ambiguous before writing the operation . - Use a bounded formation : row , arc , triangle , grid , or two rows of three . - Require full visibility and gaps ; avoid piles , cropped bodies , merged bodies , and countable reflections . - For edits , anchor the group to a region and name the smallest operation : add , remove , separate , uncrop , or clarify . - Add only the missing number or remove only the excess instances . ### Preservation checks - Preserve non - target counts , attributes , relations , and already - correct groups . - Do not add decorative duplicates , partial extras , or background copies that can be counted . ### Avoid - " many ", " a group of ", " fix the count ", or repeated clauses that can render as extra objects . ### Minimal instruction pattern Generation : " Show exactly < N > < object > total in < formation / region >, each fully visible and separated . Do not include extra , cropped , fused , reflected , or background < object >." Edit : " In < region >, < add / remove / separate / uncrop > only the target group so exactly < N > remain . Preserve correct instances and < non - target constraints >."

sections.heading: spatial_relation_layout (version 2.0.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : spatial_relation_layout ## Description Construct generation or edit instructions for static spatial relations using frame anchors , depth , support , containment , occlusion , and visibility cues . ## Instructions ### Applicable when - A constraint involves left / right , above / below , front / behind , inside / on , under , or on top of . - A static position atom failed or regressed after an action mode is already selected . ### Do not use when - The prompt only asks for attributes , style , or exact count without a static spatial relation . - The failed atom is a verb such as chasing , playing with , or jumping over ; use ‘ action_pose_relation ‘. - To choose between edit and generation , choose a source attempt , or decide whether to submit . ### Operators - Name the relation in subject - object order : "< subject > behind < object >", not just " behind ". - Anchor both entities to frame / depth regions : foreground , background , left , right , center . - For behind / in front , state depth and non - blocking occlusion . - For left / right , use viewer - frame wording . - For above / below , state vertical separation and contact / gap . - For inside / on , state containment or support contact . ### Preservation checks - Keep both entities visible . - Preserve correct counts and attributes . ### Avoid - Ambiguous words like " near ", " around ", " with ", or " interacting " without concrete visual evidence . - Contradictory relations or hiding either endpoint . ### Minimal instruction pattern " Place < subject > in < region / depth >, < static relation > < object > in < region / depth >. Keep both visible and show the relation with separation , support , containment , or occlusion cues . Preserve < non - target constraints >."

sections.heading: attribute_entity_binding (version 1.0.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : attribute_entity_binding ## Description Construct generation or edit instructions that bind color , material , texture , and identity attributes to the correct entity without leakage . ## Instructions ### Applicable when - A constraint asks whether a specific object is red , green , glass , metal , shiny , sparkling , or otherwise attribute - bound . - Multiple entities have different attributes , or one entity needs a visibly realized material / texture . ### Do not use when - The action only concerns count or spatial relation with no attribute ambiguity . - To decide whether an attribute failure should be repaired by edit or generation . ### Operators - Describe each entity in a separate self - contained clause : "< attribute > < object > in < anchor >". - Put the attribute next to the noun ; avoid floating adjective lists . - Add spatial anchors when multiple objects are present . - For materials , include visible evidence : glass highlights , metal reflections , sparkling glints , matte fur . - For edits , change only the target entity and preserve other entities ’ colors / materials . ### Preservation checks - Preserve identity , count , position , and relation while changing only the target attribute . - Do not spread the attribute to non - target objects or background props . ### Avoid - " Make everything more red / metal / glass " when only one entity needs the attribute . - Combined phrases like " red and green cats and sheep ". ### Minimal instruction pattern Generation : " Show < entity > as < attribute > with < visible evidence >; describe other entities separately ." Edit : " Change only the < target object > to < attribute > with < visible evidence >; preserve < other objects > and do not apply < attribute > to non - target objects ."

sections.heading: local_edit_preservation (version 2.0.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : local_edit_preservation ## Description Construct narrow edit instructions with explicit target operation , spatial anchor , preservation lock , and forbidden changes . ## Instructions ### Applicable when - The retry policy has already selected ‘ edit_image ‘. - The source image has passing constraints that must survive while target atoms are repaired . - Broad edits risk regressing stable atoms . ### Do not use when - The action is ‘ generate_image ‘. - No source attempt exists . - To decide whether editing is preferable to regeneration , which source attempt to use , or whether to stop . ### Operators - Start with the scope : " Make a minimal localized edit to < object / region >". - Name the target object , group , attribute , or relation . - State the smallest operation : add / remove one instance , separate merged instances , recolor one entity , adjust pose / orientation , or move one object . - Anchor the operation to a visible region or entity . - Translate preserve constraint IDs into visible counts , colors / materials , identities , layout , and relation cues . - End with forbidden changes , including full - scene redraw , unrelated style changes , or new copies . ### Preservation checks - Non - target objects remain the same type and count . - Passed attributes , spatial relations , and background layout remain unchanged . - Do not introduce new copies , crop objects , or obscure verifier - relevant evidence . ### Avoid - " Fix the image ", " improve the scene ", or broad restyling . - Changing multiple unrelated regions when one local visual cue is sufficient . ### Minimal instruction pattern " Target operation : < smallest change >. Spatial anchor : < object / region >. Preservation lock : keep < stable objects / counts / attributes / relations / layout > unchanged . Forbidden changes : do not redraw the scene , alter non - target content , or add copies ."

sections.heading: action_pose_relation (version 2.1.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : action_pose_relation For failed or uncertain verb retries , preserve exact counts , identity , attributes , and static layout ; the focal pair counts toward totals . Chasing uses one lateral pursuer / target pair . Playing uses reciprocal cross - role interaction . Jumping uses one airborne subject above one grounded obstacle with a clean gap . One scene ; each required instance appears once ; no panels . ## Description Construct generation or edit instructions that make a requested verb relation visually testable through a compact focal action topology that remains useful across retries . ## Instructions ### Operators - Chasing : lateral near - capture focal pair with asymmetric intent . - Playing with : cross - role pair uses reciprocal gaze , reach , and contact . - Jumping over : airborne subject crosses one grounded obstacle . - Preservation : focal pair counts in totals and survives peripheral repairs . - Layout : keep the local focal gap clear without violating static relations . ### Applicable when - A verb atom failed or is uncertain and the next instruction needs a different composition rather than another synonymous motion - cue rewrite . - A historical source already passes the verb and a local non - verb repair must preserve its action evidence . ### Do not use when - The task has no verb relation . - The relation is only static left / right / front / behind / under / on - top . - The failure is only count , attribute , or object identity and the selected source has no verb evidence at risk . - To choose generate versus edit , select a source attempt , override the reducer , or decide whether to submit . ### Shared focal topology - Build one decisive cross - role focal pair . The focal instances are included in the requested totals ; never add an extra demonstration pair . - Give the pair a locally clear action corridor : a small non - contact gap for chasing , a clean vertical non - contact gap for jumping , or gentle cross - role contact for playing . Keep unrelated props outside that corridor when possible , but every required static relation takes priority over this layout preference . - Continue remaining instances as separated , countable supporting participants . Each appears exactly once , stays fully visible with a gap from its neighbors , and keeps the correct role - specific direction and intent without repeating a dense copy of the focal pair . - Use one continuous scene . Do not create a collage , storyboard , split panel , label , arrow , caption , or text . ### Chasing operator - State the asymmetric roles once : ‘< subject >‘ are the pursuers and ‘< object >‘ are the fleeing targets ; never reverse or intermix the roles . - Use a lateral or three - quarter lateral action lane . Put one lead pursuer a small non - contact gap trailing one lead target along the direction of travel , not behind it in camera depth . - Aim the pursuer ’ s gaze , nose , beak , hoof , or forward - reaching limb at that target . Make the target move away and look back in alarm . - Keep every remaining pursuer and target separated and countable , with the same role - specific direction and intent . Do not force them into dense rows . - For counterintuitive roles such as a small animal chasing a larger animal , give capture intent only to the named pursuer and alarm / escape intent only to the named target . - Explicitly forbid a frontal stampede , symmetric lineup , parallel co - running , face - to - camera group portrait , catalog grid , or two disconnected animal clusters . Generic dust or blur alone is not chase evidence . - Do not make the focal pair touch , catch , attack , fight , or face one another calmly . ### Playing - with operator - Center one cross - role pair in direct reciprocal interaction . Use reciprocal gaze plus an unmistakable gentle reach or playful contact between one ‘< subject >‘ and one ‘< object >‘. - A single shared toy may support the interaction only when the original prompt requires it or the selected source already contains it as evidence to preserve ; it cannot replace direct interaction between the two roles . - Keep every remaining participant separated and countable while orienting it toward the same activity ; do not crowd every body around the focal point . - Use reciprocal gaze and relaxed , interactive poses . Avoid parallel posing , unrelated activity , or fighting . ### Jumping - over operator - Freeze one focal ‘< subject >‘ at the decisive airborne crossing directly above one grounded ‘< object >‘. - Leave a clean vertical air gap between the jumper ’ s feet / body and the obstacle . Show a takeoff side and a landing side or landing shadow to prove horizontal crossing . - Keep the obstacle grounded and fully visible . Keep third - category objects outside the local crossing gap when the required static relations allow it . - Show every required subject exactly once . Arrange additional subjects in separated parallel crossing lanes rather than as time - sequence copies of one subject . Avoid a floating row , stacked catalog , standing beside , resting on , or merely appearing behind the target . ### Verb - pass preservation - When the selected source already passes the verb , treat its focal pair , action corridor , role order , shared contact , or airborne gap as a preservation lock . - Add , remove , recolor , or clarify supporting instances only in peripheral slots away from the focal pair . - Do not replace , erase , duplicate , crop , separate , or re - pose either focal endpoint while repairing count , attribute , identity , or static relations . - Include the passed verb constraint among ‘ preserve_constraint_ids ‘ whenever an edit targets only non - verb atoms . ### Minimal instruction patterns Generation : " In one continuous scene , expand the selected typed operator into explicit pose , orientation , contact , and gap evidence for one focal < subject >/< object > pair . Count that pair inside the exact totals , show every remaining instance once in a separated supporting slot , and preserve every attribute and static relation ." Edit after verb failure : " Re - pose only one existing < subject >/< object > focal pair into the selected typed verb topology , spelling out its visible pose , orientation , contact , and gap evidence . Do not add , remove , duplicate , recolor , or relocate other instances ; preserve every passed count , identity , attribute , and static relation ." Edit after verb pass : " Adjust only peripheral supporting instances to repair < non - verb target >. Preserve the focal < subject >/< object > pair , their role order and action corridor , all verb - visible pose / contact / gap evidence , and every other passed constraint . Do not redraw or duplicate either focal endpoint ."

sections.heading: object_identity_presence (version 1.0.0).
sections.text: ⬇ # Skill : object_identity_presence ## Description Construct generation or edit instructions that make required object categories recognizable , present , fully visible , and distinct from related substitutions . ## Instructions ### Applicable when - An ‘ object ‘ atom failed or is uncertain . - A required object is missing , substituted by a related category , or too malformed or occluded to identify . ### Do not use when - The category is already clear and only count , color , material , position , or action relation is wrong . - To decide generate versus edit , choose a source attempt , or stop . ### Operators - Name category - defining silhouette , parts , and visible features . - Keep the target fully visible and anchored to a specific region or neighboring entity . - Replace or clarify only the wrong or missing target . - Exclude similar - category substitutions . - Avoid distracting copies that could break count atoms . ### Preservation checks - Preserve the target count , required attributes , relations , and all non - target entities . - Do not add props that resemble the required category . ### Minimal instruction pattern Generation : " Show a clearly recognizable < object > with < defining parts / silhouette >, fully visible ; do not substitute a related category or add distracting copies ." Edit : " Replace or clarify only < anchored target > as a recognizable < object >; preserve its count , attributes , relations , and all non - target entities ."

sections.heading: Frozen tools and a limited budget.
sections.text: The policy controls instructions and candidate choices, not the image model’s parameters. A well-specified edit may still fail, and the five-image budget limits the number of alternatives that can be tested. Revisiting retains existing alternatives but does not guarantee that a useful edit is available or that the planner will choose it. The feasible-set result in Appendix D concerns an optimal policy, not a guarantee for the trained agent.

sections.heading: Feedback and evaluation scope.
sections.text: Constraint feedback is an observation from a fixed verifier, not a guarantee of visual correctness. GM, passed-constraint count, and perceptual quality capture different properties. Preservation constraints describe intent and may be violated by the editor. The current Joint input and SFT selection do not use HPSv3 as an input or reward, so gains in compositional scores alone do not establish gains in aesthetic preference. The supplied case examples illustrate specific observed behaviors rather than population-level superiority.

sections.heading: Selective supervision and local credit.
sections.text: GM-based SFT selection can omit a temporarily degrading action even when a later descendant succeeds. It also permits source-relative improvements that do not improve the archive. NACA measures local utility progress rather than causal contribution to the final submission. Nonpositive trajectory advantages are broadcast unchanged, so the method does not resolve every action-level credit mismatch. Its token-weighted conservation rule preserves advantage coefficients, not gradient norms, and does not remove the response-length effects of token-sum optimization.

sections.heading: Protocol constraints.
sections.text: The environment determines submission eligibility and enforces mandatory stopping conditions. Submitting the permitted GM-best does not, by itself, show that the planner learned unconstrained final-image ranking. Teacher and student cases also provide different kinds of evidence: a teacher’s successful continuation is not automatically evidence that the student learned the same behavior. The evaluation uses the execution and scoring protocol in Appendix A.4 .

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.16224v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026 Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation Zixu Wang Xiaoran Zhao Yahui Liu Feng-ao Wang Junhao Xiao You Shu Bing Liu Yiting Liu Songlei Jian Zhiliang Tian Dongsheng Li NUDT PDL Lab Xiaohongshu HNU FDU SCUT SYSU Abstract Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit , an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection . The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine . We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action’s contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines. 1 Introduction Recent text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual fidelity and instruction following [ 29 , 30 , 34 ] , while satisfying object counts, attributes, and spatial relations in a single generation attempt remains challenging [ 6 , 16 ] . To address this challenge, Iterative generation uses feedback on intermediate results to guide subsequent generation and editing [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] . As iterative generation produces multiple intermediate outcomes, the appropriate corrective action may vary from round to round. Fixed refinement procedures may therefore struggle to adapt to the evolving generation process, motivating an agentic sequential decision-making formulation in which the agent learns to select the next operation based on the accumulated interaction history [ 23 ] . Figure 1: An illustrative comparison between latest-state refinement and our GenRevisit. However, these policies mainly focus on learning what action to take next. An editing operation requires both a source image ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) and an editing instruction, but the source is often predetermined by the workflow. Although the interaction history records what action has attempted on each state and the resulting feedback, it works only for revising the instruction based on the fixed state if we just learn the action selection policy. This design has room for improvement because if we can’t jointly decide continuation state and action to do, we may miss more promising state to continue for better results. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1 , an edit to I 0 I_{0} produces I 1 I_{1} but violates previously satisfied constraints. A latest-only policy then gains additional feedback, yet its next edit must still start from the degraded image I 1 I_{1} . The agent may thus spend its limited budget restoring constraints that remain satisfied in I 0 I_{0} . This highlights the need for a policy that learns to jointly select a continuation state and specify an editing instruction tailored to it, rather than only adapting the instruction to a fixed source. To this end, we introduce GenRevisit, a framework that expands decision space from action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. We treat image candidates accumulated in the interaction history as candidate continuation states, each corresponding to a possible starting point for further refinement. At each decision step, GenRevisit uses a multimodal planner to choose the next action from generation, editing, querying, and submission, based on decision context. When it edits, it jointly decides a source image and an editing instruction to correct remaining errors while preserving satisfied constraints. This allows the planner to revisit a stronger image candidate and open new refinement branches, rather than being restricted to the latest image. We train our proposed GenRevisit in two stages. First, we collect multi-round trajectories with GPT-5.5 and initialize the planner by supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We supervise actions that improve the image, including recovery from degraded states. Failed actions are excluded from the SFT loss but kept in the history with their feedback, because they still inform later decisions. We then use reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO [ 31 ] to further improve the planner through its own interactions. The terminal reward measures how well the final submitted image satisfies the task constraints. However, the standard GRPO assigns the same advantage to every action in a trajectory, so a positive trajectory advantage can reinforce actions that worsen the image. To address this issue, we propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA). In positive-advantage trajectories, NACA redistributes credit among generation and editing actions based on the fraction of the remaining utility gap that each action closes. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GenRevisit from three perspectives: (i) Compositional generation: GenRevisit achieves 84.3 GM on GenEval2 [ 16 ] , exceeding the strongest agentic baseline by 12.7 points. Results on GenEval [ 6 ] and GenEval++ [ 38 ] further support cross-benchmark generalization. (ii) Cross-generator transfer: We use GenRevisit with Z-Image-Turbo [ 39 ] without additional training. It also outperforms the strongest agentic baseline with the same generator by 10.9 points on GenEval2. (iii) Benefit of joint selection: Joint selection outperforms latest-only and best-only rules by 5.0 and 2.8 GM points, in matched-budget teacher continuations. The policy trained on joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM on GenEval2, exceeding its best-only-trained counterpart by 4.0 points. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose GenRevisit, a history-conditioned framework for joint continuation-state and action selection, making the choice of where to continue an explicit policy decision rather than a predetermined starting condition. • We combine action-level SFT with RL and introduce NACA, which redistributes image-action credit in positive-advantage trajectories according to normalized local progress. • GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++ and GenEval2 among baselines, surpassing the best GenEval2 results for Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively, showing strong compositional generation. 2 Related Work Compositional evaluation. As text-to-image models are increasingly expected to satisfy constraints involving multiple objects, attributes, and relations simultaneously, compositional faithfulness has become a core test of generation capability. Earlier benchmarks such as GenEval, T2I-CompBench, and ConceptMix organize evaluation around predefined compositional dimensions [ 6 , 11 , 35 ] , whereas TIFA, Davidsonian Scene Graph, and GenEval 2 move toward prompt-specific atomic verification by decomposing each request into individually verifiable rubrics [ 10 , 4 , 16 ] . Inspired by this paradigm, we use constraint-level atomic judgments as fine-grained environment feedback for multi-round agentic generation, allowing decisions to be grounded in how individual constraints evolve across attempts. Iterative image generation. Iterative generation has progressed from prompt rewriting, repeated editing, and visual reflection [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] to closed-loop systems that evaluate intermediate results and invoke generation or editing tools accordingly [ 36 , 9 , 13 ] . More recent approaches make this feedback loop increasingly explicit: Qwen-Image-Agent incorporates verification feedback into subsequent refinement, while R3 organizes feedback-driven retry and repair [ 40 , 33 ] . Generation Navigator further formulates iterative generation as state-dependent action selection, learning when to stop, refine, or regenerate [ 23 ] . We build on this progression by extending the decision from what to do next to which source state to act from: historical candidates are retained as selectable branching points, allowing the policy to jointly choose a source state and the subsequent operation. 3 Preliminaries Agentic image generation can be viewed as a sequential decision process in which a planning policy interacts with external tools. Given a prompt specifying multiple compositional requirements, the objective is to produce an image that satisfies these requirements within a total budget of image generation and editing calls. At each decision step, the planner selects an action according to its planning policy, conditioned on the current decision context. The environment executes the action and updates the decision context with the resulting observations and feedback. We formalize this interaction in terms of states, actions, and trajectories. States and actions. Let x x denote the input prompt and B B the total budget of image generation and editing calls. At decision step t t , the interaction state s t s_{t} denotes the decision context available to the planning policy, including x x , the available history of actions, images, and feedback, and the remaining budget. The policy π θ \pi_{\theta} , parameterized by θ \theta , selects an executable action as a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). Each action specifies an operation and its associated parameters. Here, s t s_{t} represents the overall decision context rather than an individual image candidate. Interaction trajectories. The environment executes a t a_{t} and incorporates the resulting observations and feedback into the next decision state s t + 1 s_{t+1} . The sequence of interactions forms a trajectory τ = ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , a 1 , … , s T − 1 , a T − 1 , s T ) , \tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{T-1},a_{T-1},s_{T}), where T T is the number of decision steps. The total number of generation and editing calls is bounded by B B and need not equal T T . We refer to the candidate selected for this purpose as the continuation state . Whether the continuation state is fixed to the latest candidate or explicitly selected from the interaction history is determined by the action interface. We further quantify the benefits of dynamic source selection through two experiments: Controlled teacher continuations. To quantify the benefit of joint selection, we select 200 prefixes from a pool of 800 teacher trajectories where the task remains unsolved after three image calls. Each prefix provides a shared starting history for Joint, Latest-only, and Best-only, with two image calls remaining. All three use the same teacher and interaction protocol, differing only in edit-source access. Latest-only uses the latest image, Best-only uses the current highest-GM image, and Joint selects the source together with its editing instruction. Joint achieves a mean final GM of 55.2, compared with 52.4 for Best-only and 50.2 for Latest-only. Its improvement over Best-only is 2.8 points (paired 95% CI: [0.46, 5.15]). Joint also increases the proportion of prefixes producing a new candidate above the shared prefix best from 57.0% with Best-only to 65.0%. These results support the value of joint selection beyond fixing the editing source to the current highest-scoring image. Learning from joint demonstrations. A second experiment examines whether joint demonstrations lead to better performance after SFT. An additional 800 Best-only teacher trajectories are collected using the same prompts and initial images as the Joint trajectories. The two demonstration sets are used to train separate student policies via SFT. Both policies are then evaluated on the official GenEval2 evaluation set of 800 prompts under the same evaluation protocol used for our main results. The student trained on Joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM, compared with 77.5 for its Best-only-trained counterpart, an improvement of 4.0 points (paired 95% CI: [2.81, 5.18]). The advantage is thus observed not only in controlled teacher continuations but also in the benchmark performance of the trained policies. 6 Conclusion We introduce GenRevisit, which learns to jointly select a continuation state and an action. SFT retains failed actions and outcomes as recovery context rather than supervision. NACA assigns action-level credit using normalized local progress in non-monotonic trajectories. Experiments demonstrate improved compositional generation across benchmarks and cross-generator transfer without additional planner training. Our findings suggest that an image’s value as a starting point depends on both its current constraint satisfaction and what a suitable edit can achieve, highlighting the importance of learning source selection and editing together.
